::: {.callout-note}
## What this page is about

Any case worth running for the project is too large for a single core. This page
covers how OpenFOAM spreads a case across many cores by **domain decomposition**, and
the three-step wrapper around the solver. To launch the parallel run as a batch job on
the cluster, see the [Slurm](../cluster/slurm.qmd) page; to set up the case in the
first place, the [OpenFOAM how-to](how-to.qmd).
:::

## The idea: domain decomposition

OpenFOAM parallelizes by **domain decomposition**: the mesh and fields are split into
$N$ subdomains, one per MPI rank, each solved on its own core, with the ranks
exchanging data across the subdomain boundaries. Three steps wrap the solver:

1. **Decompose** the case into $N$ pieces.
2. **Run the solver in parallel** across those pieces.
3. **Reconstruct** the pieces back into a single case for post-processing.

## Decompose, run, reconstruct

The split is controlled by `system/decomposeParDict`:

```{.cpp filename="system/decomposeParDict"}
numberOfSubdomains 4;       // = number of MPI ranks / cores
method             scotch;  // automatic, load-balanced partitioning (no manual input)
```

```bash
decomposePar                              # creates processor0/ ... processor3/
mpirun -np 4 simpleFoam -parallel | tee log.simpleFoam
reconstructPar                            # merge processor*/ back into the time directories
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## On the cluster, let Slurm launch it
Run the solver step inside a Slurm batch job: request the same number of tasks as
`numberOfSubdomains` and launch with `srun` in place of `mpirun`. See the
[Slurm](../cluster/slurm.qmd) page for the full job script.

```bash
#SBATCH --ntasks=4
srun simpleFoam -parallel
```
:::

## A few practical points

**The counts must match.** `numberOfSubdomains`, the `-np` / `--ntasks` count, and the
number of `processor*` folders `decomposePar` creates are all the *same* number. Set it
once and carry it through every step:

```{.cpp filename="system/decomposeParDict"}
numberOfSubdomains 8;       // split the case into 8 pieces
method             scotch;
```

```bash
decomposePar                        # -> processor0/ processor1/ ... processor7/  (8 folders)
mpirun -np 8 simpleFoam -parallel   # -np 8 matches the 8 subdomains
reconstructPar                      # merge the 8 pieces back together
# on the cluster:  #SBATCH --ntasks=8   then   srun simpleFoam -parallel
```

**Choosing the method.** `scotch` needs no hand-tuning: it partitions automatically for
a balanced load and is the right default. `simple` and `hierarchical` instead cut the
domain along the coordinate directions, which you may want on a structured mesh or to
keep a cut away from a sensitive region. With both, the product of the per-direction
counts in `n` must equal `numberOfSubdomains`:

```{.cpp filename="system/decomposeParDict (simple)"}
numberOfSubdomains 4;
method simple;
simpleCoeffs
{
    n (2 2 1);          // 2 cuts in x, 2 in y, 1 in z  ->  2 x 2 x 1 = 4
}
```

```{.cpp filename="system/decomposeParDict (hierarchical)"}
numberOfSubdomains 4;
method hierarchical;
hierarchicalCoeffs
{
    n     (2 2 1);      // same 4-way split ...
    order xyz;          // ... decomposed in x first, then y, then z
}
```

**Viewing without reconstructing.** You need not reconstruct to look at results:
ParaView opens a decomposed case directly (tick **Decomposed Case** in the reader), and
most `postProcess` functions run in parallel too
(e.g.\ `simpleFoam -postProcess -parallel -func ...`).

::: {.callout-important}
## Do not over-decompose
Very small subdomains spend more time communicating across their boundaries than
computing inside them, so past a point adding cores makes the run *slower*. Keep on the
order of $5\times10^{4}$ cells per core, and decompose for that target rather than for
every core you can grab.
:::

## References

The `decomposeParDict` keywords and the full set of decomposition methods are documented
in the OpenFOAM User Guide [@openfoamUserGuide].
